---
title: "Sealed Classes in C#"
---

A **`sealed`** class is a class that **cannot be inherited**. Once you mark a class as `sealed`, no other class can derive from it.


## Basic Syntax

```csharp
sealed class MyClass
{
    // This class cannot be inherited
}

// ❌ This will cause a compile-time error!
class DerivedClass : MyClass  // Error: cannot derive from sealed type
{
}
```


## Visual Concept

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    INHERITANCE CHAIN                        │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                             │
│   ┌──────────────┐                                          │
│   │   Animal     │  ◄── Base class (can be inherited)       │
│   └──────┬───────┘                                          │
│          │                                                  │
│          ▼                                                  │
│   ┌──────────────┐                                          │
│   │     Dog      │  ◄── Derived class (can be inherited)    │
│   └──────┬───────┘                                          │
│          │                                                  │
│          ▼                                                  │
│   ┌──────────────┐                                          │
│   │ sealed Poodle│  ◄── Sealed class (🔒 STOPS HERE!)       │
│   └──────────────┘                                          │
│          │                                                  │
│          ✖ No further inheritance allowed                   │
│                                                             │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```


## Example Code

```csharp
// Base class
public class Animal
{
    public virtual void Speak() => Console.WriteLine("Some sound");
}

// Derived class (can still be inherited)
public class Dog : Animal
{
    public override void Speak() => Console.WriteLine("Woof!");
}

// Sealed class - inheritance STOPS here
public sealed class Poodle : Dog
{
    public override void Speak() => Console.WriteLine("Fancy Woof!");
}

// ❌ Compile Error: 'Labradoodle': cannot derive from sealed type 'Poodle'
// public class Labradoodle : Poodle { }
```


## Sealed Methods

You can also seal **individual methods** in a derived class to prevent further overriding:

```csharp
public class Animal
{
    public virtual void Move() => Console.WriteLine("Moving...");
}

public class Bird : Animal
{
    // This method cannot be overridden in derived classes
    public sealed override void Move() => Console.WriteLine("Flying!");
}

public class Penguin : Bird
{
    // ❌ Error: cannot override sealed method
    // public override void Move() => Console.WriteLine("Waddling!");
}
```


## Best Use Cases

### 1. **Security & Integrity**

Prevent malicious or unintended modifications to critical classes:

```csharp
public sealed class PasswordValidator
{
    public bool Validate(string password)
    {
        // Critical validation logic that shouldn't be bypassed
        return password.Length >= 8 
            && password.Any(char.IsUpper)
            && password.Any(char.IsDigit);
    }
}
```


### 2. **Immutable Data Classes**

Ensure immutability cannot be broken by inheritance:

```csharp
public sealed class PatientRecord
{
    public string PatientId { get; }
    public string Name { get; }
    public DateTime DateOfBirth { get; }

    public PatientRecord(string id, string name, DateTime dob)
    {
        PatientId = id;
        Name = name;
        DateOfBirth = dob;
    }
}
```


### 3. **Utility/Helper Classes**

Classes with only static methods don't need inheritance:

```csharp
public sealed class DicomHelper
{
    public static string ParsePatientName(string dicomTag) 
    {
        // Parse DICOM patient name format
        return dicomTag.Replace("^", " ").Trim();
    }

    public static double ConvertHounsfieldToLinear(double hu)
    {
        return (hu + 1024) / 1024.0;
    }
}
```


### 4. **Performance Optimization**

The .NET runtime can optimize sealed classes because it knows no derived types exist:

```csharp
public sealed class FastImageProcessor
{
    // JIT compiler can use direct method calls (devirtualization)
    // instead of virtual method dispatch
    public void ProcessPixel(int x, int y)
    {
        // High-performance pixel processing
    }
}
```


### 5. **API Design - Prevent Extension**

When you want to control exactly how your library is used:

```csharp
// You provide these specific report types
public abstract class RadiologyReport { }

public sealed class CTReport : RadiologyReport { }
public sealed class MRIReport : RadiologyReport { }
public sealed class XRayReport : RadiologyReport { }

// Users cannot create: class CustomReport : CTReport { }
```


## Real-World Examples in .NET

Many .NET framework classes are sealed:

```csharp
// These are all sealed in .NET:
string    // System.String is sealed
DateTime  // System.DateTime is sealed (struct, implicitly sealed)
int       // System.Int32 is sealed (struct)
```


## Summary Table

| Aspect | Sealed Class | Regular Class |
|--------|--------------|---------------|
| Can be inherited? | ❌ No | ✅ Yes |
| Performance | 🚀 Slightly faster (devirtualization) | Normal |
| Security | 🔒 More secure | Can be extended |
| Flexibility | Less flexible | More flexible |


## When to Use `sealed`

```
Use sealed when:
├── ✅ Security/integrity is critical
├── ✅ Class is immutable and should stay that way  
├── ✅ Class has no virtual members (nothing to override)
├── ✅ You want to prevent breaking changes in derived classes
└── ✅ Performance matters (hot paths in code)

Avoid sealed when:
├── ❌ You're building a framework meant to be extended
├── ❌ You want to allow customization via inheritance
└── ❌ Unit testing requires mocking (sealed classes are harder to mock)
```
